- Anomaly hunting reads data the system already produced; it finds bugs no test case anticipated and is best on long-lived databases, before demos, and after migrations or releases.
- Eight families: impossible values, column contradictions, table contradictions, impossible time, sentinels/placeholders, statistical outliers, suspicious regularity, absence.

- Impossible time: completed-in-future, paid future month, future attendance, pay before hire month; also updated_at < created_at, child before parent, approval after leave; allow a time-zone margin.
- Sentinels/placeholders (1970-01-01, 9999-12-31, 0, N/A, test) and leaked test data before demos.
- z-score outliers (STDDEV_POP): excluded invalid rows first, 17.5 h scored 2.43; caveats: one outlier inflates the deviation, small samples need robust methods, compute per group; the 4 h Saturday is caught by a rule, not by statistics.
- Regularity: rows created in the same second, identical times, unchanged payslips, sudden volume jumps.
- Absence needs anti-joins/calendars (HR department has no active staff).

chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Anomaly hunting is testing without a script
Scripted tests check the behaviours you thought of. Anomaly queries do the opposite: they read the data the system has already produced and ask "does this make sense?" Every bug that ever ran against a database (a missing validation, a race condition, a bad import, a hand-run fix) left fingerprints in it. So the cheapest defects to find are the ones already stored, and this technique is the best return on investment on a long-lived QA or staging database, before a demo, after a migration, and after a release. It also finds the bugs your test cases can't, because nobody wrote a test for the scenario that caused them.
## Eight families of anomaly
Most data problems fall into a handful of families. Naming them tells you which question to ask of any table:
Family
The question
| Example in our data | Impossible values | Is any value outside what reality allows? | Net pay of -2000, a 17.5-hour day | Column contradictions |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Do columns in one row disagree? | A request that ends before it starts | Table contradictions | Do related tables disagree? | Status says approved, history says pending |
| Impossible time | Does the timeline break? | Completed in the future, paid before hire | Sentinels and placeholders | Are "no value" markers pretending to be data? |
| 1970-01-01, 0, N/A, test | Statistical outliers | Is one value far from its peers? | One 6-day request among 1 to 3 day requests | Suspicious regularity |
| Too identical, too clustered, too many at once? | Fifty rows created in the same second | Absence | Should something exist that doesn't? | An active employee with no attendance for a day |

The first six are "something is there that shouldn't be", and the last is "something isn't there that should be", which is harder to see because there is no row to look at.
## Start with a profile, then ask what looks wrong
Before writing any rule, look at the shape of the data (8.6). A distribution query is the fastest way to spot values that don't belong:

| SELECT days, | COUNT(*)                                         AS requests, | ROUND(100 * COUNT(*) / SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (), 1) AS pct |
|---|---|---|
| FROM   leave_requests | GROUP  BY days | ORDER  BY days; |

days | requests | pct
| 1.0  \| 3        \| 21.4 | 2.0  \| 7        \| 50.0 |
|---|---|
| 3.0  \| 3        \| 21.4 | 6.0  \| 1        \| 7.1 |

Half the requests are two days, and one request is six. That's not a bug (request 4 spans a year-end week), but a value that appears once deserves a "why?", and here the answer is a legitimate long holiday. The percentages sum to 99.9 because of rounding, which is worth remembering when you compare a pie chart's legend with the data (5.5). Run the same query on every low-cardinality column (statuses, types, categories) and every numeric column you can bucket.
## Impossible and out-of-range values: a range probe across many columns
One query with a UNION ALL (5.4) gives you the minimum, the maximum and the count of suspicious values for several fields at once:
```sql
SELECT 'payroll.net_pay' AS field,
       MIN(net_pay) AS min_val, MAX(net_pay) AS max_val, SUM(net_pay <= 0) AS suspicious
FROM   payroll
```
| UNION ALL | SELECT 'attendance.hours', | MIN(ROUND(TIME_TO_SEC(TIMEDIFF(check_out, check_in)) / 3600, 2)), | MAX(ROUND(TIME_TO_SEC(TIMEDIFF(check_out, check_in)) / 3600, 2)), | SUM(TIME_TO_SEC(TIMEDIFF(check_out, check_in)) / 3600 <= 0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| OR TIME_TO_SEC(TIMEDIFF(check_out, check_in)) / 3600 > 16) | FROM   attendance WHERE check_in IS NOT NULL AND check_out IS NOT NULL | UNION ALL | SELECT 'leave_requests.days', MIN(days), MAX(days), SUM(days <= 0 OR days > 30) | FROM   leave_requests; |

| field               \| min_val  \| max_val  \| suspicious | payroll.net_pay     \| -2000.00 \| 67000.00 \| 1 |
|---|---|
| attendance.hours    \| -8.00    \| 17.50    \| 2 | leave_requests.days \| 1.0      \| 6.0      \| 0 |

Each line names a rule ("net pay must be positive", "a day is between 0 and 16 hours", "leave is 1 to 30 days") and counts the rows breaking it. The thresholds come from the requirement or a conversation with the analyst, and a threshold you invent is just a guess. Notice -8.00: a negative duration is what a check-out before a check-in looks like, so the same defect can show up in a range probe and a contradiction check.
## Contradictions: cross-tabulate two columns that should move together
When two columns are linked by a rule, a cross-tab (3.2) shows the whole relationship at once, and the wrong cells stand out:

| SELECT status, | SUM(approved_by IS NOT NULL) AS with_approver, | SUM(approved_by IS NULL)     AS without_approver |
|---|---|---|
| FROM   leave_requests | GROUP  BY status | ORDER  BY status; |

| status   \| with_approver \| without_approver | approved \| 7             \| 0 |
|---|---|
| pending  \| 0             \| 6 | rejected \| 1             \| 0 |

The healthy pattern is block-diagonal: decided requests have a decider, pending ones don't. A non-zero in approved / without_approver or pending / with_approver would be an anomaly, and here both are zero. The same idea works for status × is_deleted, payment_status × paid_amount > 0, type × required_field_is_null, or status × last history status. It is quicker than writing eight separate violation queries, and it shows you combinations you didn't think to forbid.
## Impossible time: nothing can happen before it exists or after "now"
Events must respect the timeline. Compare each timestamp with "now" (@now, frozen) and with the dates of the entities they belong to:
```sql
SELECT 'appointment completed before it starts' AS anomaly, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM   appointments WHERE status = 'completed' AND starts_at > @now
UNION ALL
SELECT 'payroll processed/paid for a future month', COUNT(*)
FROM   payroll
WHERE  status IN ('processed','paid') AND pay_month > DATE_FORMAT(@today, '%Y-%m-01')
UNION ALL
SELECT 'attendance dated in the future', COUNT(*)
FROM   attendance WHERE work_date > @today
UNION ALL
SELECT 'payroll for a month before the hire month', COUNT(*)
FROM   payroll p JOIN employees e ON e.employee_id = p.employee_id
WHERE  p.pay_month < DATE_FORMAT(e.hire_date, '%Y-%m-01');
```

anomaly                                     | n
| appointment completed before it starts      \| 1 | payroll processed/paid for a future month   \| 1 |
|---|---|
| attendance dated in the future              \| 0 | payroll for a month before the hire month   \| 1 |

Other timeline rules worth a query: updated_at < created_at, a child created before its parent, a history row earlier than the record it describes, an approval dated after the leave it approves, and a resignation date before the hire date. Time-zone offsets (1.2) can make a correct row look "in the future" by a few hours, so use a margin such as one day before calling it a defect.
## Sentinels and placeholders: "no value" dressed as a value
Systems fill gaps with defaults: 1970-01-01, 1900-01-01, 9999-12-31, 0, -1, '', 'N/A', 'unknown', 'test'. They pass IS NOT NULL checks and quietly poison reports (an average tenure that includes 56 years of "1970" hires). Sweep for them, and look for test data leaking into a demo or staging environment:
```sql
SELECT employee_id, first_name, last_name, email
FROM   employees
WHERE  LOWER(CONCAT_WS(' ', first_name, last_name, email)) REGEXP 'test|dummy|asdf|xxx|lorem|sample|demo|temp|n/a';
-- 0 rows on our sample data
```

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS suspicious_dates FROM employees WHERE hire_date IN ('1900-01-01', '1970-01-01', '9999-12-31');   -- 0
```

Also check the numeric side (how many rows have exactly 0 in a column that should never be zero) and the text side (the most frequent values in each free-text column; a spike on '.' or '-' is someone getting past a required-field rule). This is the natural home of the "leaked test data" check before a client demo (the Vatsalya-style HRMS demo scenario): search names, emails and notes for the strings your own team uses.
## Statistical outliers: z-scores and their limits
A z-score says how many standard deviations a value is from the average. Rows beyond 2 or 3 deserve a look. Hours worked per day, on valid rows only:
```sql
WITH h AS (
  SELECT attendance_id, employee_id, work_date,
         TIME_TO_SEC(TIMEDIFF(check_out, check_in)) / 3600 AS hours
  FROM   attendance
  WHERE  check_in IS NOT NULL AND check_out IS NOT NULL AND check_out > check_in
```
| ), | s AS (SELECT AVG(hours) AS mu, STDDEV_POP(hours) AS sd FROM h) |
|---|---|
| SELECT h.attendance_id, h.employee_id, h.work_date, | ROUND(h.hours, 2)                    AS hours, |
| ROUND((h.hours - s.mu) / s.sd, 2)    AS z_score | FROM   h CROSS JOIN s |
| WHERE  ABS(h.hours - s.mu) / s.sd > 2 | ORDER  BY ABS(h.hours - s.mu) DESC; |

attendance_id | employee_id | work_date  | hours | z_score
104           | 2           | 2026-09-17 | 17.50 | 2.43

The average is 8.84 hours, the standard deviation 3.56. Four caveats keep you honest. The impossible row (check-out before check-in) was excluded first, or it would distort the average. The 4-hour Saturday (row 103) has a z-score of only -1.36, so it is not flagged, and it is caught by the weekend rule instead, which shows that statistics and business rules find different things. One extreme value inflates the standard deviation and can hide itself, so on small samples use a robust method (median plus median absolute deviation, or NTILE(4) / PERCENT_RANK() from 5.5). And compute the score within a sensible group (per employee, per department, per shift), otherwise a night-shift worker looks like an outlier next to everyone on days. STDDEV_POP is population standard deviation (STDEVP in SQL Server, stddev_pop in PostgreSQL), and STDDEV_SAMP gives slightly different scores.
## Suspicious regularity: too identical, too clustered
## Real activity is messy. Perfect regularity means machines, imports or copy-paste:
-- Rows created in the same second (a bulk load, seed script or import)
```sql
SELECT created_at, COUNT(*) AS rows_created
```
| FROM   employee_documents | GROUP  BY created_at |
|---|---|
| HAVING COUNT(*) > 1; | -- one row: your timestamp \| 4       (the four seed rows were inserted by one statement) |

Related patterns: check-in times identical to the second across weeks, every appointment starting exactly on the hour, a payslip that never changes for 24 months, a sudden jump in rows per day (GROUP BY DATE(created_at) with LAG, 5.5), a column whose distinct count fell after a release, and a user who performs hundreds of actions a minute. Each is an invitation to ask "which path produced this?"
## Absence: the anomaly with no row to show
Missing things need an anti-join or a calendar (4.1, 5.2), because you're looking for a hole:
```sql
SELECT d.name AS department, COUNT(e.employee_id) AS active_staff
FROM   departments d
LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.department_id = d.department_id AND e.status = 'active' AND e.is_deleted = 0
GROUP  BY d.department_id, d.name
HAVING COUNT(e.employee_id) = 0;
```

department | active_staff
## HR         | 0

The only HR employee is resigned, so no active person can handle HR approvals, which is a data condition worth asking about (10.5 shows what it does to workflows). The heavier absence checks (attendance days that never got a row, payroll rows missing for a closed month, completed appointments with no charge) are templates in 10.3.
## Triage: not every anomaly is a bug
Each result needs a verdict, because a list of unexplained findings gets ignored:

| Verdict | Meaning | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Defect | The system produced data it shouldn't | Report with the query, rows and impact |
| Legitimate exception | Rare but allowed (a 6-day leave) | Note it, add an allowance to the check if it will recur |
| Legacy or migrated data | Predates the rule | Ask whether to fix, and baseline it (10.2) |
| Test debris | Left by a run or a demo | Clean up with the tag-based script (7.2) |
| Unknown | Nobody can say | Ask the analyst; don't guess |

## Trace the source before you report
The strongest bug report says how the row got there. Clues sit in the row itself (created_by, created_at, updated_at) and in the pattern across violating rows. Group the violations by day and by creator, then line the days up against release dates:
-- Template: when did this start, and who or what produced it?
```sql
SELECT DATE(created_at) AS day, created_by, COUNT(*) AS violating_rows
FROM   <table> WHERE <violation condition>
GROUP  BY DATE(created_at), created_by
ORDER  BY day;
```

A cluster starting the day after a deployment points at that release, one creator (or a service account) points at an import or job, and rows spread evenly over months point at an old, long-standing gap. This is where the audit columns from 8.4 pay off, and where a missing created_by becomes a finding in its own right.
## From anomaly to a permanent test
A found anomaly should become three things. A negative test that tries to recreate it through the UI or API. A regression check in the scoreboard (10.2). And, where it's a structural gap, a constraint proposal (8.1). The negative test looks like this:
```ts
test('an appointment that has not started cannot be marked completed', async ({ request }) => {
  const [before]: any = await db.execute('SELECT status FROM appointments WHERE appointment_id = 101');
```

```ts
  const res = await request.patch('/api/appointments/101', { data: { status: 'completed' } });
  expect(res.status()).toBe(422);                              // refused with a validation error, not 200 and not 500
```

```ts
  const [after]: any = await db.execute('SELECT status FROM appointments WHERE appointment_id = 101');
  expect(after[0].status).toBe(before[0].status);              // and the row is unchanged
});
```

The Selenium equivalent drives the same action through the page and then asserts on a pymysql query. Whichever tool you use, the final assertion belongs to the database.
## A starter kit for any table
When you meet a table for the first time (8.6), run this list of questions against it:

| Question | Pattern |
|---|---|
| Are required-in-practice columns empty? | COUNT(*) versus COUNT(col) |
| Do text values have stray spaces or case variants? | col <> TRIM(col), LOWER(TRIM(col)) groups (2.5) |
| Any negative or zero amounts, quantities, durations? | Range probe |
| Any dates in the future or the distant past? | MIN/MAX, sentinel list |
| Which values appear exactly once? | Distribution query |
| Which combinations never or always occur together? | Cross-tab of two columns |
| Duplicates on the business key? | GROUP BY ... HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 |
| Rows with no parent or no child? | Anti-joins (4.3) |
| Does the status agree with its history? | Latest-history comparison (6.3) |
| Outliers in each numeric column? | z-score within a group |
| Rows created in clusters? | GROUP BY created_at |
| Reference values never used? | Left join lookups to users |

chapters.customSummary:
- A check = one rule, returns violating rows (evidence), deterministic (parameters such as @today), read-only, cheap, traceable (id, rule, source, severity, owner, params).
- Store as files in Git (review, CI) or as rows in qa_checks (in-database scheduling); layout with checks/, guards/, baseline.yml, runner.
- SQL-only runner (MySQL): qa_checks + qa_check_results + sp_run_sanity_checks using PREPARE, COUNT(*) INTO @n, max_allowed baseline; sample run: 4 FAIL, 1 baselined PASS, 1 PASS; double-quoted SQL text unless ANSI_QUOTES.
- pytest runner: one test per .sql file, strip semicolons, wrap with SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (...) with the paren on its own line, evidence rows in the failure message, JUnit output for CI (9.4).
- Baselines with reason and expiry; fail only on increases (and optionally on decreases); expired baselines fail.
- Test the checks: insert a bad row in a rolled-back transaction and expect the hit (mutation testing for queries); guard checks for wrong environment, empty tables, stale data.
- Runner safety: SET SESSION TRANSACTION READ ONLY, max_execution_time, read-only account on a replica, LIMIT on evidence, off-hours for heavy checks.
- Store results per run and watch trends (LAG per check); post failures with id, severity, count and sample rows.
- Keep the library healthy: owners, review dates, a check per bug found, review never-failing and forever-failing checks, near-zero false positives.
- Dialect notes: PG EXECUTE/DO, SQL Server sp_executesql; the external runner is the most portable.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## From one-off queries to a library
Everything in Parts 4 to 6 and 10.1 produced queries you ran once. The value multiplies when they become a suite: named, documented, parameterised checks that anyone on the team can run after a deployment, a data refresh, a migration or before a demo, and get the same answer. This chapter is about the engineering that makes that work, and it is the foundation of the mini-project in 12.3 and the pipeline stage in 9.4.
## Anatomy of a good check
A check is one rule expressed as a query that returns the violating rows. Empty means pass. Return rows and not just a count, because the rows are the evidence for the bug report, and you can always count them. Every check carries a header:
-- id:        LEV-002
-- rule:      An employee must not have two pending/approved leave requests whose dates overlap.
-- source:    REQ-LV-014 (leave policy, section 3.2)
-- severity:  high
-- owner:     qa-team          last reviewed: 2026-09-21
-- params:    none
-- returns:   one row per overlapping pair (empty result = pass)
```sql
SELECT a.leave_request_id AS request_a, b.leave_request_id AS request_b, a.employee_id,
       a.start_date AS a_start, a.end_date AS a_end, b.start_date AS b_start, b.end_date AS b_end
```
| FROM   leave_requests a | JOIN   leave_requests b ON  b.employee_id = a.employee_id |
|---|---|
| AND a.leave_request_id < b.leave_request_id | AND a.start_date <= b.end_date AND b.start_date <= a.end_date |

## request_a | request_b | employee_id | a_start    | a_end      | b_start    | b_end
9         | 101       | 1           | 2026-10-12 | 2026-10-13 | 2026-10-13 | 2026-10-14

## Rules that keep checks trustworthy:
One rule per check. A check that tests three things fails for three different reasons, and nobody can tell which.
Return keys and the columns needed to understand the row, not SELECT *.
Deterministic. No NOW() or CURRENT_DATE inside the query. Use parameters (@today) so a rerun tomorrow gives the same answer.
Read-only and cheap. Indexed filters, no functions on filtered columns (2.1), and no full scan of a huge table without a date window.
Traceable. Every check names the requirement or decision behind it, so when it fires, people know why the rule exists.
Graded. Severity says how loudly to complain: critical (money or legal: payroll), high (workflow correctness), medium, low.
A rule of thumb for what belongs in the library: it protects something expensive, it has broken before, or it can't be enforced by a constraint.
Files in Git or rows in a table
Two common homes, with different strengths:

| Files in a repository | Rows in a qa_checks table |
|---|---|
| Review and history | Pull requests, blame, diffs |
| Manual | Run from CI and pytest |
| Natural | Needs a small runner |
| Run inside the database (scheduled job) | Awkward |
| Natural | Works with a read-only account |
| Yes | Only if the account can read the table |

A practical layout for the file approach:
| sanity/ | checks/ | ATT-001_checkout_without_checkin.sql | LEV-002_overlapping_leave.sql | PAY-001_net_pay_vs_components.sql |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| guards/ | GRD-001_environment_identity.sql | baseline.yml            # accepted known issues, each with a reason and an expiry | run_checks.py           # the runner | README.md               # how to run, how to add a check, severity meanings |

## A SQL-only runner (MySQL)
If you can create objects in a QA schema, keep the checks in a table and run them with a small stored procedure. Each check stores the SQL that returns the violating rows, and the procedure counts them. This uses dynamic SQL (PREPARE), so treat it as an internal tool, not a pattern for application code.
```sql
CREATE TABLE qa_checks (
```
| check_id    VARCHAR(20)  PRIMARY KEY, | module      VARCHAR(20)  NOT NULL, | severity    ENUM('critical','high','medium','low') NOT NULL, | description VARCHAR(150) NOT NULL, | sql_text    TEXT         NOT NULL,          -- returns the violating rows |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| max_allowed INT          NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, -- accepted known issues (see baselines below) | is_enabled  TINYINT(1)   NOT NULL DEFAULT 1, | owner       VARCHAR(40)  NULL, | note        VARCHAR(200) NULL | ); |

```sql
CREATE TABLE qa_check_results (
```
| result_id  INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, | run_id     CHAR(36)    NOT NULL, | check_id   VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL, |
|---|---|---|
| violations INT         NOT NULL, | run_at     DATETIME    NOT NULL | ); |

```sql
INSERT INTO qa_checks (check_id, module, severity, description, sql_text, max_allowed, owner, note) VALUES
('ATT-001','attendance','high',  'Check-out recorded without a check-in',
 "SELECT attendance_id FROM attendance WHERE check_in IS NULL AND check_out IS NOT NULL", 0, 'qa-team', NULL),
('ATT-002','attendance','medium','Check-in without check-out on a past day',
 "SELECT attendance_id FROM attendance WHERE check_in IS NOT NULL AND check_out IS NULL AND work_date < @today", 1, 'qa-team', 'Known: auto-close job not deployed (BUG-482)'),
('LEV-001','leave','high',       'Approved leave request without an approver',
 "SELECT leave_request_id FROM leave_requests WHERE status = 'approved' AND approved_by IS NULL", 0, 'qa-team', NULL),
('LEV-002','leave','high',       'Overlapping pending/approved leave for one employee',
 "SELECT a.leave_request_id, b.leave_request_id AS other_id FROM leave_requests a JOIN leave_requests b ON b.employee_id = a.employee_id AND a.leave_request_id < b.leave_request_id AND a.start_date <= b.end_date AND b.start_date <= a.end_date WHERE a.status IN ('pending','approved') AND b.status IN ('pending','approved')", 0, 'qa-team', NULL),
('PAY-001','payroll','critical', 'Net pay differs from basic + allowances - deductions',
 "SELECT payroll_id FROM payroll WHERE basic_salary + allowances - deductions <> net_pay", 0, 'qa-team', NULL),
('PAY-002','payroll','critical', 'More than one payroll row for an employee and month',
 "SELECT employee_id, pay_month FROM payroll GROUP BY employee_id, pay_month HAVING COUNT(*) > 1", 0, 'qa-team', NULL);
```

The check text is wrapped in double quotes so the SQL inside can use single quotes. This works unless your server runs with ANSI_QUOTES in sql_mode. The runner:
```sql
DELIMITER //
CREATE PROCEDURE sp_run_sanity_checks()
```
| BEGIN | DECLARE done INT DEFAULT 0; | DECLARE v_id  VARCHAR(20); |
|---|---|---|
| DECLARE v_sql TEXT; | DECLARE cur CURSOR FOR SELECT check_id, sql_text FROM qa_checks WHERE is_enabled = 1 ORDER BY check_id; | DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND SET done = 1; |

  IF @today IS NULL THEN SET @today = CURRENT_DATE(); END IF;   -- checks reference @today
  SET @run_id = UUID();

| OPEN cur; | read_loop: LOOP |
|---|---|
| FETCH cur INTO v_id, v_sql; | IF done = 1 THEN LEAVE read_loop; END IF; |

    SET @n = NULL;
    SET @stmt_sql = CONCAT('SELECT COUNT(*) INTO @n FROM (', v_sql, ') AS violating_rows');
    PREPARE s FROM @stmt_sql;
    EXECUTE s;
    DEALLOCATE PREPARE s;

```sql
    INSERT INTO qa_check_results (run_id, check_id, violations, run_at) VALUES (@run_id, v_id, @n, NOW());
  END LOOP;
  CLOSE cur;
```

## Running from outside the database: a pytest runner
A test framework gives you reporting, CI integration and parameterisation for free. Each .sql file becomes one test, and the runner counts the rows and compares with the baseline:
# sanity/run_checks.py
```ts
import pathlib, datetime, pytest, yaml
```

CHECKS   = sorted(pathlib.Path("sanity/checks").glob("*.sql"))
BASELINE = yaml.safe_load(open("sanity/baseline.yml")) or {}

```py
def run(db, sql):
    sql = sql.strip().rstrip(";")                           # comments/semicolons would break the wrapper
    db.execute("SET @today = %s", ("2026-09-21",))          # frozen date: same answer on every run
    db.execute(f"SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (\n{sql}\n) AS v")     # the closing paren is on its own line: a trailing -- comment can't swallow it
    return db.fetchone()[0]
```

```py
@pytest.mark.parametrize("path", CHECKS, ids=lambda p: p.stem)
def test_sanity_check(db, path):
    check_id = path.stem.split("_")[0]                      # "LEV-002_overlapping_leave" -> "LEV-002"
    sql      = path.read_text()
    allowed  = 0
    if check_id in BASELINE:
        entry = BASELINE[check_id]
        assert entry["expires"] >= datetime.date.today(), f"baseline for {check_id} expired: {entry['reason']}"
        allowed = entry["allowed"]
```

    n = run(db, sql)
## if n > allowed:
        db.execute(f"SELECT * FROM (\n{sql.strip().rstrip(';')}\n) AS v LIMIT 20")   # evidence in the failure message
        pytest.fail(f"{check_id}: {n} violation(s), {allowed} allowed.\nFirst rows: {db.fetchall()}")

# sanity/baseline.yml
ATT-002: {allowed: 1, reason: "Auto-close job not deployed (BUG-482)", expires: 2026-10-31}

Run it with pytest sanity -q --junitxml=sanity.xml. Every CI system displays JUnit results, which turns your checks into pipeline test cases (9.4). A Node version with mysql2 and glob works the same way.
## Baselines: fail only on increases, and make exceptions expire
Shared databases always have a few known-bad rows (6.3), and a suite that is always red is ignored. The answer is a baseline: for each check, the number of accepted violations, plus a reason and an expiry date. The runner fails when the count goes above the baseline, and also fails when a baseline expires, so an exception can't quietly become permanent. Also fail when a count drops below the baseline, in a "strict" mode, so someone reduces the baseline when a defect is fixed, which keeps the suite honest.
## Test your checks: prove each one can fail
A check that never fires is either a healthy system or a broken query. You can't tell which without trying. The technique is the query equivalent of mutation testing: inside a transaction, create the bad row, run the check, expect a hit, and roll back (7.3):
```py
def test_LEV_001_detects_an_approved_request_with_no_approver(db):
    db.execute("START TRANSACTION")
    db.execute("""INSERT INTO leave_requests (employee_id, leave_type_id, start_date, end_date, days, status)
                  VALUES (1, 1, '2027-01-11', '2027-01-11', 1, 'approved')""")
    n = run(db, pathlib.Path("sanity/checks/LEV-001_approved_without_approver.sql").read_text())
    db.execute("ROLLBACK")
    assert n == 1
```

Do this at least once when you write a check, and again when you change it. Also add guard checks that make the suite itself trustworthy:
-- GRD-001: the suite must be pointed at the environment you think it is
```sql
SELECT DATABASE() AS db, @@hostname AS host
WHERE  DATABASE() <> 'hrms_practice';                 -- adjust per environment: empty = correct target
```

-- GRD-002: a check on an empty table passes for the wrong reason
```sql
SELECT 'leave_requests is empty' AS problem FROM (SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM leave_requests) t WHERE n = 0;
```

-- GRD-003: freshness. Attendance data should not be older than 3 days at the run date
```sql
SELECT MAX(work_date) AS latest_attendance FROM attendance HAVING MAX(work_date) < @today - INTERVAL 3 DAY;
```

An empty result passes, like every check. Guards catch the classic silent failures: the suite pointed at the wrong database, a nightly sync that stopped, or a refreshed environment that arrived empty (in which case every "no violations" is meaningless).
## Keep the runner safe
A sanity runner should never be able to change data, and never hurt the database. Layered protections:
```sql
SET SESSION TRANSACTION READ ONLY;                                    -- MySQL: any write in this session errors
SET SESSION max_execution_time = 30000;                               -- MySQL: SELECTs longer than 30 s are cancelled
-- PostgreSQL:  SET default_transaction_read_only = on;  SET statement_timeout = '30s';
-- SQL Server:  use a read-only login and a client-side command timeout (pyodbc timeout, mssql requestTimeout)
```

Better still, use a read-only database account (0.5) on a replica (11.2). Add a LIMIT to evidence queries, schedule heavy checks off-hours, and give each check a time budget so one slow rule doesn't stall the suite.

| Report results and watch the trend | Store every run, then look at movement, not just the latest snapshot: |
|---|---|
| SELECT check_id, run_at, violations, | violations - LAG(violations) OVER (PARTITION BY check_id ORDER BY run_at) AS change_since_previous |
| FROM   qa_check_results | ORDER  BY check_id, run_at; |

A count that climbs after a release is a regression even if it's still under a lenient threshold, and a count that has sat at 3 for a year is a debt you can quantify. Post failures to the team channel with the check id, severity, count and the first few evidence rows, and link the check file so the reader can see the rule.
## Keeping the library healthy
A library rots unless someone owns it. Give each check an owner and a review date, revisit checks when a requirement changes (a rule that used to be true becomes a false alarm), add a check for every defect found ("bug found, check added"), and track two signals: checks that have never failed in a long time (are they still meaningful, and do they still work per the mutation test?) and checks that have failed for months (should they be fixed, or accepted with a baseline and a date?). Keep false positives at nearly zero, because a check that cries wolf trains people to ignore the whole suite.
## Dialect notes
The rule queries are nearly portable, and the runner differs. On PostgreSQL, wrap dynamic SQL in EXECUTE inside a DO block or a function, or, more simply, use the external runner. On SQL Server use sp_executesql. WEEKDAY, DATE_FORMAT, TIMESTAMPDIFF and TIME_TO_SEC in these Part 10 queries are MySQL, and the equivalents are in Appendix B. That the external runner works against any database, with only the .sql files changing per dialect, is the strongest argument for it.

## How to use these templates
Each module below gives you three layers: an integrity scoreboard (rules that should never be broken, one row per rule), completeness and calculation checks (things that should exist, numbers that should add up), and expected-value queries for the screens and reports you test. Copy the ones that match your rules, replace names and thresholds, and confirm every assumption (working days, grace periods, cut-off dates) with the analyst. Every threshold in these templates is a placeholder for a requirement.
Attendance
The integrity scoreboard
```sql
SELECT 'ATT-01 check-out without check-in' AS check_name, COUNT(*) AS violations
FROM   attendance WHERE check_in IS NULL AND check_out IS NOT NULL
UNION ALL
SELECT 'ATT-02 check-in without check-out (past day)', COUNT(*)
FROM   attendance WHERE check_in IS NOT NULL AND check_out IS NULL AND work_date < @today
UNION ALL
SELECT 'ATT-03 check-out not after check-in', COUNT(*)
FROM   attendance WHERE check_in IS NOT NULL AND check_out IS NOT NULL AND check_out <= check_in
UNION ALL
SELECT 'ATT-04 punches on an approved leave day', COUNT(*)
FROM   attendance a
WHERE  (a.check_in IS NOT NULL OR a.check_out IS NOT NULL)
  AND  EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM leave_requests lr
               WHERE lr.employee_id = a.employee_id AND lr.status = 'approved'
```
| AND a.work_date BETWEEN lr.start_date AND lr.end_date) | UNION ALL |
|---|---|
| SELECT 'ATT-05 punches on a weekend or holiday', COUNT(*) | FROM   attendance a |
| WHERE  (a.check_in IS NOT NULL OR a.check_out IS NOT NULL) | AND  (WEEKDAY(a.work_date) >= 5 OR a.work_date IN (SELECT holiday_date FROM company_holidays)) |
| UNION ALL | SELECT 'ATT-06 more than 16 hours in one day', COUNT(*) |
| FROM   attendance | WHERE  check_in IS NOT NULL AND check_out IS NOT NULL |
| AND  TIME_TO_SEC(TIMEDIFF(check_out, check_in)) > 16 * 3600 | UNION ALL |
| SELECT 'ATT-07 attendance before hire date', COUNT(*) | FROM   attendance a JOIN employees e ON e.employee_id = a.employee_id WHERE a.work_date < e.hire_date |
| UNION ALL | SELECT 'ATT-08 attendance for inactive or deleted employee', COUNT(*) |

| check_name                                        \| violations | ATT-01 check-out without check-in                 \| 1 | ATT-02 check-in without check-out (past day)     \| 1 |
|---|---|---|
| ATT-03 check-out not after check-in               \| 1 | ATT-04 punches on an approved leave day           \| 1 | ATT-05 punches on a weekend or holiday            \| 1 |
| ATT-06 more than 16 hours in one day              \| 1 | ATT-07 attendance before hire date                \| 0 | ATT-08 attendance for inactive or deleted employee \| 0 |

Each of the six hits is a different defect: row 3 (no check-in), row 2 (no check-out), row 101 (check-out before check-in), row 102 (Mina punching on approved sick leave), row 103 (a Saturday) and row 104 (17.5 hours). Rows that only have NULL punches on an approved leave day, like employee 1 on 15 September, are correctly not counted, because a leave day is expected to have an empty row. Duplicate attendance rows can't appear here since the table has UNIQUE (employee_id, work_date), but do test that the app handles a double check-in gracefully (8.1).
## Completeness: working days with no row
A calendar built with a recursive CTE (5.2) lists every working day, and an anti-join finds who has no record and no reason (leave):
SET @from = '2026-09-14', @to = '2026-09-18';

| WITH RECURSIVE cal AS ( | SELECT CAST(@from AS DATE) AS d | UNION ALL |
|---|---|---|
| SELECT d + INTERVAL 1 DAY FROM cal WHERE d < @to | ), | workdays AS ( |
| SELECT d FROM cal | WHERE  WEEKDAY(d) < 5 AND d NOT IN (SELECT holiday_date FROM company_holidays) | ) |
| SELECT w.d AS work_date, e.employee_id, CONCAT(e.first_name, ' ', e.last_name) AS employee | FROM   workdays w | JOIN   employees e ON e.status = 'active' AND e.is_deleted = 0 AND e.hire_date <= w.d |
| LEFT JOIN attendance a ON a.employee_id = e.employee_id AND a.work_date = w.d | WHERE  a.attendance_id IS NULL | AND  NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM leave_requests lr |
| WHERE lr.employee_id = e.employee_id AND lr.status = 'approved' | AND w.d BETWEEN lr.start_date AND lr.end_date) | ORDER  BY w.d, e.employee_id; |

| work_date  \| employee_id \| employee | 2026-09-16 \| 3           \| Mina Thapa | 2026-09-17 \| 3           \| Mina Thapa |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-09-18 \| 1           \| Asha Karki | 2026-09-18 \| 2           \| Ravi Shrestha | 2026-09-18 \| 3           \| Mina Thapa |

Look at the pattern, and not just the rows. Mina is missing two days that could be absences, but 18 September is missing for everyone. When the same date is empty for every employee, an individual explanation ("they were all absent") is unlikely, and a systemic one (the sync job didn't run, the import failed) is far more probable. Group by date and it jumps out: GROUP BY w.d gives 1, 1, 3. That difference between individual and systemic gaps is exactly what a good tester notices.
## Expected values for the daily attendance screen
The report screen for one employee turns each day into a status. Encode the requirement (grace period, label priority) in a CASE, and use the result as the expected column:

| WITH RECURSIVE cal AS ( | SELECT CAST(@from AS DATE) AS d | UNION ALL |
|---|---|---|
| SELECT d + INTERVAL 1 DAY FROM cal WHERE d < @to | ) | SELECT c.d AS work_date, a.check_in, a.check_out, |
| ROUND(TIME_TO_SEC(TIMEDIFF(a.check_out, a.check_in)) / 3600, 2) AS hours, | CASE | WHEN a.attendance_id IS NULL                          THEN 'No record' |
| WHEN a.check_in IS NULL AND a.check_out IS NULL       THEN 'No punches' | WHEN a.check_in IS NOT NULL AND a.check_out IS NULL   THEN 'Missing check-out' | WHEN a.check_in > '09:15:00'                          THEN 'Late'          -- grace period: 15 minutes (assumption) |
| ELSE 'Present' | END AS day_status | FROM   cal c |
| LEFT JOIN attendance a ON a.employee_id = 2 AND a.work_date = c.d | WHERE  WEEKDAY(c.d) < 5 | ORDER  BY c.d; |

| work_date  \| check_in \| check_out \| hours \| day_status | 2026-09-14 \| 09:20:00 \| NULL      \| NULL  \| Missing check-out | 2026-09-15 \| 09:10:00 \| 17:40:00  \| 8.50  \| Present |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-09-16 \| 09:45:00 \| 17:20:00  \| 7.58  \| Late | 2026-09-17 \| 06:00:00 \| 23:30:00  \| 17.50 \| Present | 2026-09-18 \| NULL     \| NULL      \| NULL  \| No record |

Two things to notice. On the 17th the "correct" status is Present, yet 17.5 hours is impossible, so the status logic and the integrity check answer different questions, and both must pass. And the label priority (a missing check-out beats "Late", so the 14th isn't reported as late) is a requirement, so ask what the label should be when two conditions hold. Weekly hours per employee are the same idea aggregated (valid rows only, so bad rows can't distort the total):

| SELECT employee_id, | COUNT(*)                                                    AS valid_days, | ROUND(SUM(TIME_TO_SEC(TIMEDIFF(check_out, check_in))) / 3600, 2) AS total_hours |
|---|---|---|
| FROM   attendance | WHERE  work_date BETWEEN '2026-09-14' AND '2026-09-18' AND check_in IS NOT NULL AND check_out > check_in | GROUP  BY employee_id ORDER BY employee_id; |

| employee_id \| valid_days \| total_hours | 1           \| 2          \| 16.98 |
|---|---|
| 2           \| 3          \| 33.58 | 3           \| 1          \| 8.17 |

## What to confirm before trusting these
Time zones (punches stored in UTC show odd offsets, 1.2), night shifts (a check-out after midnight needs a datetime, not a TIME), rounding rules for minutes, grace periods, half days, regularisation requests that legitimately edit punches, and rosters that override the default weekday calendar (which the roster feature in the HR dashboard may drive).
Payroll
The integrity scoreboard
```sql
SELECT 'PAY-01 net pay differs from components' AS check_name, COUNT(*) AS violations
FROM   payroll WHERE basic_salary + allowances - deductions <> net_pay
UNION ALL
SELECT 'PAY-02 duplicate row for employee + month', COUNT(*)
FROM  (SELECT 1 FROM payroll GROUP BY employee_id, pay_month HAVING COUNT(*) > 1) d
UNION ALL
SELECT 'PAY-03 net pay zero or negative', COUNT(*) FROM payroll WHERE net_pay <= 0
UNION ALL
SELECT 'PAY-04 processed/paid for a future month', COUNT(*)
FROM   payroll WHERE status IN ('processed','paid') AND pay_month > DATE_FORMAT(@today, '%Y-%m-01')
UNION ALL
SELECT 'PAY-05 pay month before hire month', COUNT(*)
FROM   payroll p JOIN employees e ON e.employee_id = p.employee_id
WHERE  p.pay_month < DATE_FORMAT(e.hire_date, '%Y-%m-01')
UNION ALL
SELECT 'PAY-06 payroll for inactive/deleted employee', COUNT(*)
FROM   payroll p JOIN employees e ON e.employee_id = p.employee_id
WHERE  e.status <> 'active' OR e.is_deleted = 1
UNION ALL
SELECT 'PAY-07 active employee missing from a closed month', COUNT(*)
FROM  (SELECT m.pay_month, e.employee_id
       FROM  (SELECT '2026-07-01' AS pay_month UNION ALL SELECT '2026-08-01') m       -- the closed months in scope
       CROSS JOIN employees e
       WHERE e.status = 'active' AND e.is_deleted = 0
         AND DATE_FORMAT(e.hire_date, '%Y-%m-01') <= m.pay_month
         AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM payroll p WHERE p.employee_id = e.employee_id AND p.pay_month = m.pay_month)) x
UNION ALL
SELECT 'PAY-08 month mixes draft with processed/paid rows', COUNT(*)
FROM  (SELECT pay_month FROM payroll GROUP BY pay_month
       HAVING SUM(status = 'draft') > 0 AND SUM(status <> 'draft') > 0) y;
```

check_name                                        | violations
PAY-01 net pay differs from components            | 1
PAY-02 duplicate row for employee + month         | 1
| PAY-03 net pay zero or negative                   \| 1 | PAY-04 processed/paid for a future month          \| 1 | PAY-05 pay month before hire month                \| 1 |
|---|---|---|
| PAY-06 payroll for inactive/deleted employee      \| 1 | PAY-07 active employee missing from a closed month \| 0 | PAY-08 month mixes draft with processed/paid rows \| 1 |

Two things to notice. PAY-03 finds row 23 but PAY-01 doesn't, because that row's net pay is the correct arithmetic (45,000 + 3,000 - 50,000 = -2,000). A calculation can be right and the situation still impossible, since deductions exceeded gross pay, which is why rules and arithmetic are separate checks. And PAY-06 returns Bikash's row, but whether it's a defect depends on when he left, which the sample table doesn't record, so this one is a question for the analyst as much as a finding. PAY-07 uses a hard-coded list of closed months. Replace it with the months your requirement says are closed, and prefer an explicit list over "everything before this month", so a month with no rows at all is still caught.

| Control totals per month | SELECT pay_month, | COUNT(*)                                          AS payroll_rows, | COUNT(DISTINCT employee_id)                       AS employees, |
|---|---|---|---|
| SUM(basic_salary + allowances - deductions)       AS expected_net, | SUM(net_pay)                                      AS stored_net, | SUM(basic_salary + allowances - deductions) - SUM(net_pay) AS difference | FROM   payroll GROUP BY pay_month ORDER BY pay_month; |

| pay_month  \| payroll_rows \| employees \| expected_net \| stored_net \| difference | 2025-02-01 \| 1            \| 1         \| 43500.00     \| 43500.00   \| 0.00 | 2026-07-01 \| 3            \| 3         \| 168000.00    \| 168000.00  \| 0.00 |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-08-01 \| 5            \| 4         \| 238500.00    \| 237500.00  \| 1000.00 | 2026-09-01 \| 1            \| 1         \| -2000.00     \| -2000.00   \| 0.00 | 2026-11-01 \| 1            \| 1         \| 57500.00     \| 57500.00   \| 0.00 |

August shows both alarms at once: five rows for four employees (the duplicate) and a 1,000 difference (the underpaid row). Compare these numbers with the payroll summary screen and with the bank file or export total, and remember that aggregates can cancel errors out (3.1), so keep the row-level checks too.
## Month-over-month changes and gaps
Pay should change for a reason. Flag every change beyond a threshold, and every month-to-month jump that isn't exactly one month:
```sql
WITH s AS (
  SELECT payroll_id, employee_id, pay_month, net_pay,
         LAG(net_pay) OVER w AS prev_net
```
| FROM   payroll | WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY employee_id ORDER BY pay_month, payroll_id) |
|---|---|
| ) | SELECT employee_id, pay_month, prev_net, net_pay, |
| net_pay - prev_net                                    AS change_amt, | ROUND(100 * (net_pay - prev_net) / ABS(prev_net), 2)  AS change_pct |
| FROM   s | WHERE  prev_net IS NOT NULL AND prev_net <> 0 |
| AND  ABS(net_pay - prev_net) / ABS(prev_net) > 0.01               -- threshold: 1% (a requirement decides the real number) | ORDER  BY employee_id, pay_month; |

employee_id | pay_month  | prev_net | net_pay  | change_amt | change_pct
2           | 2026-09-01 | 43500.00 | -2000.00 | -45500.00  | -104.60
3           | 2026-08-01 | 67000.00 | 66000.00 | -1000.00   | -1.49

```sql
WITH s AS (
  SELECT payroll_id, employee_id, pay_month,
         PERIOD_DIFF(EXTRACT(YEAR_MONTH FROM pay_month),
                     EXTRACT(YEAR_MONTH FROM LAG(pay_month) OVER (PARTITION BY employee_id ORDER BY pay_month, payroll_id)))
```
| AS months_since_previous | FROM   payroll |
|---|---|
| ) | SELECT employee_id, payroll_id, pay_month, months_since_previous |

| employee_id \| payroll_id \| pay_month  \| months_since_previous | 1           \| 22         \| 2026-11-01 \| 3 |
|---|---|
| 2           \| 5          \| 2026-07-01 \| 17 | 2           \| 7          \| 2026-08-01 \| 0 |

A gap of 0 means a repeated month (the duplicate), a gap above 1 means missing months (employee 1 jumps from August to a November row that is itself invalid). The two queries together separate "the amount looks wrong" from "the timeline looks wrong."

```ts
  expect(rows).toHaveLength(1);                         // a duplicate row would make the screen's source ambiguous
  const c = (v: string) => Math.round(Number(v) * 100);
  expect(ui).toEqual({ basic: c(rows[0].basic_salary), allow: c(rows[0].allowances),
                       ded: c(rows[0].deductions),     net: c(rows[0].net_pay) });
  expect(ui.net).toBe(ui.basic + ui.allow - ui.ded);    // and the screen's own arithmetic holds
});
```

Compare money in integer minor units (cents or paisa), never as floats (1.2, 3.1), and read the string the database returns before converting. Also freeze paid months: once a month is paid, its rows must never change, and a before/after snapshot (6.6) around any "recalculate" or data-fix action proves it.
## What to confirm before trusting these
The rounding rule for statutory items and taxes (2.4), whether deductions can legitimately exceed gross pay in a final settlement, when a month counts as closed, whether inactive employees can receive a last payment, and which statuses a month may mix during a run (PAY-08 is informational until the process says otherwise).
Appointments
The integrity scoreboard
```sql
SELECT 'APT-01 ends at or before its start' AS check_name, COUNT(*) AS violations
FROM   appointments WHERE ends_at <= starts_at
UNION ALL
SELECT 'APT-02 duration differs from the service duration', COUNT(*)
FROM   appointments a JOIN services s ON s.service_id = a.service_id
WHERE  TIMESTAMPDIFF(MINUTE, a.starts_at, a.ends_at) <> s.duration_min
UNION ALL
SELECT 'APT-03 provider double-booked', COUNT(*)
FROM   appointments a
JOIN   appointments b ON b.employee_id = a.employee_id AND a.appointment_id < b.appointment_id
                     AND a.starts_at < b.ends_at AND b.starts_at < a.ends_at
WHERE  a.status IN ('booked','completed') AND b.status IN ('booked','completed')
UNION ALL
SELECT 'APT-04 completed but not started yet', COUNT(*)
FROM   appointments WHERE status = 'completed' AND starts_at > @now
UNION ALL
SELECT 'APT-05 still booked after the start time', COUNT(*)
FROM   appointments WHERE status = 'booked' AND starts_at < @now
UNION ALL
SELECT 'APT-06 booking uses an inactive service', COUNT(*)
FROM   appointments a JOIN services s ON s.service_id = a.service_id
WHERE  a.status = 'booked' AND s.is_active = 0
UNION ALL
SELECT 'APT-07 booking assigned to an inactive/deleted provider', COUNT(*)
FROM   appointments a JOIN employees e ON e.employee_id = a.employee_id
WHERE  a.status = 'booked' AND (e.status <> 'active' OR e.is_deleted = 1)
UNION ALL
SELECT 'APT-08 provider on approved leave', COUNT(*)
FROM   appointments a
WHERE  a.status IN ('booked','completed')
  AND  EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM leave_requests lr
               WHERE lr.employee_id = a.employee_id AND lr.status = 'approved'
                 AND DATE(a.starts_at) BETWEEN lr.start_date AND lr.end_date);
```

| check_name                                             \| violations | APT-01 ends at or before its start                     \| 1 | APT-02 duration differs from the service duration      \| 2 |
|---|---|---|
| APT-03 provider double-booked                          \| 1 | APT-04 completed but not started yet                   \| 1 | APT-05 still booked after the start time               \| 1 |
| APT-06 booking uses an inactive service                \| 1 | APT-07 booking assigned to an inactive/deleted provider \| 1 | APT-08 provider on approved leave                      \| 1 |

The overlap test uses strict inequalities (<), because an appointment ending at 10:30 and another starting at 10:30 do not clash, unlike date-only leave (4.2). Appointment 103 shows up twice (APT-01 and APT-02), since a negative duration also differs from the service's duration, so report it once and reference both checks. APT-05 uses the frozen @now, and running it against a live clock will change the answer every minute. APT-06 looks only at booked rows on purpose: an inactive service is fine on completed history and wrong on a new booking.
The ledger checks
Money attached to appointments needs its own rules:
```sql
SELECT 'LED-01 completed appointment without a charge' AS check_name, COUNT(*) AS violations
```
| FROM   appointments a | WHERE  a.status = 'completed' |
|---|---|
| AND  NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM appointment_ledger l WHERE l.appointment_id = a.appointment_id AND l.entry_type = 'charge') | UNION ALL |
| SELECT 'LED-02 charge differs from the service price', COUNT(*) | FROM   appointment_ledger l |
| JOIN   appointments a ON a.appointment_id = l.appointment_id | JOIN   services     s ON s.service_id     = a.service_id |
| WHERE  l.entry_type = 'charge' AND l.amount <> s.price | UNION ALL |
| SELECT 'LED-03 more than one charge for an appointment', COUNT(*) | FROM  (SELECT appointment_id FROM appointment_ledger WHERE entry_type = 'charge' |
| GROUP BY appointment_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1) x | UNION ALL |
| SELECT 'LED-04 payments exceed charges', COUNT(*) | FROM  (SELECT appointment_id, |
| SUM(CASE WHEN entry_type = 'charge'  THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS charged, | SUM(CASE WHEN entry_type = 'payment' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS paid |
| FROM   appointment_ledger GROUP BY appointment_id) t | WHERE  t.paid > t.charged; |

check_name                                     | violations
| LED-01 completed appointment without a charge  \| 1 | LED-02 charge differs from the service price   \| 1 |
|---|---|
| LED-03 more than one charge for an appointment \| 1 | LED-04 payments exceed charges                 \| 1 |

LED-01 is appointment 104 (the same one that was completed in the future), LED-02 is ledger row 3 (1,200 charged against a 1,500 price), LED-03 is appointment 3 (two 800 charges), and LED-04 is appointment 108 (1,500 paid against 1,200 charged). Whether the price on the ledger must equal today's services.price is a requirement question (prices change, and history should keep the price at the time), so confirm it before reporting LED-02.
## A running balance per customer
A ledger screen shows a running total. Rebuild it with a window function (5.5) and compare it line by line:
```sql
SELECT c.full_name AS customer, l.ledger_id, l.entry_type, l.amount,
       CASE l.entry_type WHEN 'payment' THEN -l.amount ELSE l.amount END AS signed_amount,
       SUM(CASE l.entry_type WHEN 'payment' THEN -l.amount ELSE l.amount END)
         OVER (PARTITION BY c.customer_id ORDER BY l.created_at, l.ledger_id) AS running_balance
```
| FROM   appointment_ledger l | JOIN   appointments a ON a.appointment_id = l.appointment_id |
|---|---|
| JOIN   customers    c ON c.customer_id    = a.customer_id | ORDER  BY c.customer_id, l.created_at, l.ledger_id; |

customer      | ledger_id | entry_type | amount  | signed_amount | running_balance
| Rajan Pandey  \| 3         \| charge     \| 1200.00 \| 1200.00       \| 1200.00 | Rajan Pandey  \| 4         \| payment    \| 1500.00 \| -1500.00      \| -300.00 |
|---|---|
| Sunita Basnet \| 1         \| charge     \| 800.00  \| 800.00        \| 800.00 | Sunita Basnet \| 5         \| charge     \| 800.00  \| 800.00        \| 1600.00 |

Rajan's balance is negative (a credit for a payment he shouldn't have needed to make), and Sunita is charged 1,600 for an 800 service. The sign convention (refunds increase what is owed) is an assumption, and the running balance at the last entry must equal the customer's outstanding-balance figure elsewhere in the app. Always use the unique ledger_id as a tiebreaker in the window's ORDER BY, or two entries in the same second give an unstable balance (5.5).
Schedule and slot checks for the calendar screen
The provider's day view is a filtered, sorted list:
```sql
SELECT a.appointment_id, TIME(a.starts_at) AS starts, TIME(a.ends_at) AS ends,
```
| c.full_name AS customer, s.name AS service, a.status | FROM   appointments a | JOIN   customers c ON c.customer_id = a.customer_id |
|---|---|---|
| JOIN   services  s ON s.service_id  = a.service_id | WHERE  a.employee_id = 2 AND DATE(a.starts_at) = '2026-09-22' AND a.status IN ('booked','completed') | ORDER  BY a.starts_at, a.appointment_id; |

| appointment_id \| starts   \| ends     \| customer     \| service      \| status | 1              \| 10:00:00 \| 10:30:00 \| Anita Sharma \| Consultation \| booked |
|---|---|
| 101            \| 10:15:00 \| 10:45:00 \| Anita Sharma \| Consultation \| booked | 2              \| 11:00:00 \| 12:00:00 \| Rajan Pandey \| Full Checkup \| booked |

Anita appears in two overlapping bookings with the same provider, so a customer double-booking check (the APT-03 join keyed on customer_id) would fire here too. On big tables, replace DATE(a.starts_at) = '...' with a range on starts_at so an index can be used (2.1). To test slot availability, the expected set of free slots is the working hours minus the union of booked intervals, and the boundary cases are the same list you'd test for leave: back-to-back bookings, one minute of overlap, a booking that spans the lunch break, and one that ends after closing.
## What to confirm before trusting these
Whether a cancelled or no_show appointment frees the slot and what it charges, whether providers can be double-booked on purpose (parallel services), time zones on starts_at, how long a booked appointment may remain before an auto-close job runs, and whether ledger amounts follow the price at booking time or today's price.

chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Leave is the richest module for data checks
Leave touches dates, business calendars, balances, approvals and other modules, so almost every earlier technique appears here. The templates are grouped by the question they answer. Parameters: @today, and the leave year 2026-01-01 to 2027-01-01 (replace with the company's leave-year rule).
## Rules to write down first
Before any query, agree on these with the analyst, because each changes the expected values:

| Rule | Assumption used below |
|---|---|
| Working week | Monday to Friday |
| Holidays | Rows in company_holidays never count as leave days |
| Leave year | Calendar year |
| Entitlement | leave_types.days_per_year per employee (no proration, no carry-forward) |
| What consumes balance | Approved requests only (pending and rejected don't) |
| Overlap | Two active (pending/approved) requests may not share a date |

## Balance reconciliation: entitlement minus approved leave
The stored balance must equal what the approved requests imply. Return only the mismatches:
```sql
SELECT b.employee_id, lt.name AS leave_type, lt.days_per_year AS entitlement,
```
| COALESCE(u.used, 0)                                AS approved_days, | lt.days_per_year - COALESCE(u.used, 0)             AS expected_balance, | b.balance                                          AS stored_balance, | b.balance - (lt.days_per_year - COALESCE(u.used, 0)) AS difference | FROM   leave_balances b | JOIN   leave_types lt ON lt.leave_type_id = b.leave_type_id |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| LEFT JOIN (SELECT employee_id, leave_type_id, SUM(days) AS used | FROM   leave_requests | WHERE  status = 'approved' AND start_date >= '2026-01-01' AND start_date < '2027-01-01' | GROUP  BY employee_id, leave_type_id) u | ON u.employee_id = b.employee_id AND u.leave_type_id = b.leave_type_id | WHERE  b.balance <> lt.days_per_year - COALESCE(u.used, 0); |

employee_id | leave_type | entitlement | approved_days | expected_balance | stored_balance | difference
3           | Sick       | 12          | 2.0           | 10.0             | 12.0           | 2.0

Mina's approved sick leave (request 8) was never deducted. The LEFT JOIN matters: an employee with no approved leave still has an expected balance (the full entitlement), and an inner join would hide exactly those rows (4.1). To see the running balance behind a single balance, rebuild the ledger for one employee and type (5.5):
```sql
SELECT lr.leave_request_id, lr.start_date, lr.days,
       SUM(lr.days) OVER (ORDER BY lr.start_date, lr.leave_request_id)                         AS used_so_far,
       lt.days_per_year - SUM(lr.days) OVER (ORDER BY lr.start_date, lr.leave_request_id)      AS balance_after
FROM   leave_requests lr
JOIN   leave_types lt ON lt.leave_type_id = lr.leave_type_id
WHERE  lr.employee_id = 2 AND lr.leave_type_id = 2 AND lr.status = 'approved'
  AND  lr.start_date >= '2026-01-01' AND lr.start_date < '2027-01-01'
ORDER  BY lr.start_date, lr.leave_request_id;
```

| leave_request_id \| start_date \| days \| used_so_far \| balance_after | 7                \| 2026-06-10 \| 2.0  \| 2.0         \| 10.0 |
|---|---|
| 6                \| 2026-07-20 \| 1.0  \| 3.0         \| 9.0 | 105              \| 2026-09-30 \| 1.0  \| 4.0         \| 8.0 |

The last line (8.0) equals Ravi's stored sick balance, and each intermediate line is what a leave-ledger screen should display. Also check that no pending demand exceeds what remains:
```sql
SELECT p.employee_id, p.leave_type_id, p.pending_days, b.balance
FROM  (SELECT employee_id, leave_type_id, SUM(days) AS pending_days
       FROM leave_requests WHERE status = 'pending' GROUP BY employee_id, leave_type_id) p
JOIN   leave_balances b ON b.employee_id = p.employee_id AND b.leave_type_id = p.leave_type_id
WHERE  p.pending_days > b.balance;              -- 0 rows: nobody has asked for more than they have
```

## Days: stored value versus the calendar
The stored days must equal the working days in the range, minus holidays. Generate each date in each request and count the ones that count:
```sql
WITH RECURSIVE d AS (
  SELECT leave_request_id, start_date AS dt, end_date FROM leave_requests
  UNION ALL
  SELECT leave_request_id, dt + INTERVAL 1 DAY, end_date FROM d WHERE dt < end_date
),
w AS (
  SELECT leave_request_id, COUNT(*) AS working_days
  FROM   d
  WHERE  WEEKDAY(dt) < 5 AND dt NOT IN (SELECT holiday_date FROM company_holidays)
```
| GROUP  BY leave_request_id | ) |
|---|---|
| SELECT lr.leave_request_id, lr.employee_id, lr.start_date, lr.end_date, | lr.days AS stored_days, COALESCE(w.working_days, 0) AS expected_days, lr.status |
| FROM   leave_requests lr | LEFT JOIN w ON w.leave_request_id = lr.leave_request_id |
| WHERE  lr.days <> COALESCE(w.working_days, 0) | ORDER  BY lr.leave_request_id; |

leave_request_id | employee_id | start_date | end_date   | stored_days | expected_days | status
1                | 2           | 2026-10-05 | 2026-10-07 | 3.0         | 2             | pending
4                | 3           | 2026-12-24 | 2026-12-31 | 6.0         | 5             | pending
102              | 3           | 2026-09-28 | 2026-09-29 | 3.0         | 2             | pending

Three findings, of two different kinds. Request 102 is a plain counting error (a Monday and a Tuesday can't be 3 days). Requests 1 and 4 only disagree once holidays are considered (6 October and 25 December fall inside them), so the finding is either "the app ignores company holidays" or "the rule doesn't exclude them", and a requirement decides which. This is why 6.3's weekday-only check passed on these two requests earlier. The LEFT JOIN also keeps a request made entirely of non-working days, whose expected count is 0.
## Overlaps and conflicts
The overlap self join (4.2) is the check shown in full in 10.2 (LEV-002, one pair: requests 9 and 101). The boundary cases to test through the UI, and that the query already encodes, are worth writing down as test data:

| Scenario | Expected | New request ends the day before an existing one starts | Allowed | New request starts on the day an existing one ends | Rejected (shares a day) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| New request fully inside an existing one | Rejected | New request fully contains an existing one | Rejected | Identical dates and type | Rejected |
| Overlaps only a rejected or cancelled request | Allowed | Overlaps a pending request of the same employee | Rejected (pending counts) | Different employee, same dates | Allowed |

Now the cross-module conflicts, where leave meets attendance and appointments:
```sql
SELECT e.employee_id, CONCAT(e.first_name, ' ', e.last_name) AS employee, a.work_date AS on_date,
       CONCAT('punches during approved leave (request ', lr.leave_request_id, ')') AS conflict
FROM   attendance a
JOIN   leave_requests lr ON lr.employee_id = a.employee_id AND lr.status = 'approved'
```
| AND a.work_date BETWEEN lr.start_date AND lr.end_date | JOIN   employees e ON e.employee_id = a.employee_id |
|---|---|
| WHERE  a.check_in IS NOT NULL OR a.check_out IS NOT NULL | UNION ALL |
| SELECT e.employee_id, CONCAT(e.first_name, ' ', e.last_name), DATE(ap.starts_at), | CONCAT(ap.status, ' appointment ', ap.appointment_id, ' during approved leave (request ', lr.leave_request_id, ')') |
| FROM   appointments ap | JOIN   leave_requests lr ON lr.employee_id = ap.employee_id AND lr.status = 'approved' |
| AND DATE(ap.starts_at) BETWEEN lr.start_date AND lr.end_date | JOIN   employees e ON e.employee_id = ap.employee_id |
| WHERE  ap.status IN ('booked','completed') | ORDER  BY employee_id, on_date; |

## employee_id | employee   | on_date    | conflict
1           | Asha Karki | 2026-09-15 | completed appointment 108 during approved leave (request 2)
3           | Mina Thapa | 2026-05-04 | punches during approved leave (request 8)

The rule that must hold across modules is the same sentence in each: an approved leave day means no punches and no appointments for that person. Approving leave after a booking exists (the reverse order) is a workflow test for the appointment side: does the app warn, move or cancel the booking?
Pending and stuck requests
```sql
SELECT leave_request_id, employee_id, start_date, created_at,
       DATEDIFF(@today, DATE(created_at)) AS days_waiting,
       CASE WHEN start_date < @today THEN 'start date already passed' ELSE 'waiting more than 7 days' END AS issue
FROM   leave_requests
WHERE  status = 'pending' AND (created_at < @today - INTERVAL 7 DAY OR start_date < @today)
ORDER  BY leave_request_id;
```

## leave_request_id | employee_id | start_date | created_at          | days_waiting | issue
4                | 3           | 2026-12-24 | 2026-09-01 09:00:00 | 20           | waiting more than 7 days
104              | 3           | 2026-09-07 | 2026-09-01 09:00:00 | 20           | start date already passed

Request 104 is the worse one, since the employee's leave dates have gone by with no decision. Test what the app does about it: escalation to a higher approver, auto-expiry, or a reminder, and check the data afterwards. The "7 days" is a service-level number from the requirement.
Who is out on a date, and how much capacity is left
SET @on_date = '2026-09-30';

```sql
SELECT d.name AS department,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees x WHERE x.department_id = d.department_id AND x.status = 'active' AND x.is_deleted = 0) AS active_staff,
       COUNT(DISTINCT lr.employee_id) AS on_approved_leave
```
| FROM   departments d | LEFT JOIN employees      e  ON e.department_id = d.department_id |
|---|---|
| LEFT JOIN leave_requests lr ON lr.employee_id  = e.employee_id AND lr.status = 'approved' | AND @on_date BETWEEN lr.start_date AND lr.end_date |
| GROUP  BY d.department_id, d.name | ORDER  BY d.department_id; |

| department \| active_staff \| on_approved_leave | Finance    \| 1            \| 0 |
|---|---|
| QA         \| 2            \| 1 | HR         \| 0            \| 0 |

Two techniques at work: the correlated subquery counts staff independently of the join, so the fan-out from leave rows can't inflate it (4.1), and COUNT(DISTINCT ...) guards the other count. This is the expected value for a team-calendar or "minimum staffing" rule, and it is a good place to test the rule at the boundary (one person left, the last person requesting leave).
## Leave dates as test data
When you seed or drive leave scenarios, cover the calendar's awkward shapes: a single day, a range spanning a weekend, a range containing a holiday, a range starting on Saturday or ending on Sunday, a range crossing a month end and a year end (a year-end request touches two leave years), a request with a start date in the past, an end date before the start date (the trigger from 8.3 refuses it), a half day (if supported), and a request for exactly the remaining balance, then one half-day above it.
```ts
test('leave applied through the UI stores the holiday-aware day count', async ({ page }) => {
| await page.goto('/leave/new'); | await page.getByLabel('Leave type').selectOption('Annual'); | await page.getByLabel('From').fill('2026-10-05'); |
|---|---|---|
| await page.getByLabel('To').fill('2026-10-07');                // Mon to Wed, Tuesday is a company holiday | await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' }).click(); | await expect(page.getByText('Leave request submitted')).toBeVisible(); |
```

```ts
  const [rows]: any = await db.execute(
    `SELECT days FROM leave_requests WHERE employee_id = ? ORDER BY leave_request_id DESC LIMIT 1`, [TEST_EMPLOYEE_ID]);
  expect(Number(rows[0].days)).toBe(2);                          // the requirement: holidays don't count
});
```

The expected value comes from the requirement (and the calendar query above), not from a formula copied out of the application's code.

chapters.contentMarkdown:
## A workflow is a state machine, and data can break it
A leave request, a payroll run and an appointment all move through states: pending → approved, booked → completed, draft → processed → paid. The rules that govern the moves (which states may follow which, who may make each move, what must happen as a side effect) are enforced by application code, and rarely by the database (8.4). Bugs here don't crash anything, they corrupt the record's history. This chapter shows how to check a workflow in three ways: after the fact from the data, in advance by generating a test for every possible transition, and around the edges, meaning who acts, when, and what else changes.
## Write the rules down as data
You can't check transitions against a rule nobody wrote down. The leave_status_transitions table (from the setup) is the state machine as rows, and the leave history table (5.5, 6.3) is the record of what actually happened:
```sql
SELECT from_status, to_status FROM leave_status_transitions ORDER BY from_status, to_status;
```

| from_status \| to_status | (new)       \| pending | approved    \| cancelled |
|---|---|---|
| pending     \| approved | pending     \| cancelled | pending     \| rejected |

rejected and cancelled have no outgoing arrows: they are terminal states. Getting this table agreed with the analyst is half the value, because vague rules ("can a rejected request be reopened?") become explicit questions.
## Illegal transitions in the history
Join every history row to the rules, and keep the rows with no matching rule:
```sql
SELECT h.history_id, h.leave_request_id, h.old_status, h.new_status, h.changed_by, h.changed_at
```

## Generate the transition test matrix from the rules
A complete workflow test is every pair of states, expected valid or invalid. Let SQL build it with a CROSS JOIN (4.1) so the test plan can't drift from the rules table:
```sql
SELECT f.s AS from_status, t.s AS to_status,
       CASE WHEN x.from_status IS NULL THEN 'INVALID' ELSE 'VALID' END AS expected
FROM  (SELECT 'pending' AS s UNION ALL SELECT 'approved' UNION ALL SELECT 'rejected' UNION ALL SELECT 'cancelled') f
CROSS JOIN
      (SELECT 'pending' AS s UNION ALL SELECT 'approved' UNION ALL SELECT 'rejected' UNION ALL SELECT 'cancelled') t
LEFT JOIN leave_status_transitions x ON x.from_status = f.s AND x.to_status = t.s
ORDER  BY FIELD(f.s, 'pending','approved','rejected','cancelled'), FIELD(t.s, 'pending','approved','rejected','cancelled');
```

The 16 rows condense to this grid (ok = valid, - = must be refused):
```py

| pending    \|   -     \|   ok     \|   ok     \|   ok | approved   \|   -     \|   -      \|   -      \|   ok |
|---|---|
| rejected   \|   -     \|   -      \|   -      \|   - | cancelled  \|   -     \|   -      \|   -      \|   - |
```

That's 4 valid moves and 12 that must be refused, including the four "no-op" self transitions, which are the ones testers usually skip. Add the creation edge (new) → pending for a fifth valid case. A test that only covers the happy path checks 1 of these 17 possibilities.

## Concurrency and repeat safety
Workflows are where race conditions bite (7.7). Repeat each valid transition with two simultaneous callers, and with one caller sending the same request twice (an idempotent retry): expect exactly one winner, one history row, one balance change, and a clean conflict message for the loser. Then run the scoreboard from 10.2 afterwards and compare with the baseline, since duplicates, broken chains and status/history mismatches are the typical residue.
## Putting it together as a repeatable workflow suite
The five queries above (illegal transitions, broken chains, status/history mismatch, actor rules, duplicate decisions) go into the sanity library with ids WFL-001 to WFL-005, run after every workflow test batch and every deployment. The generated matrix drives the API tests, the role matrix drives the authorisation tests, and the side-effect table becomes the assertion list. When the analyst changes a rule, you edit one table of rows, and the queries and tests follow.
